item.title: 2 coaching rumors — Houston Rockets, Milwaukee Bucks (Aug 14)
item.description:
Milwaukee Bucks · Aug 14, 11:05 UTC · via New York Times
Doc Rivers’ career coaching the Orlando Magic (1999-2004), Celtics (2004-2013), Clippers (2013-2020), Philadelphia 76ers (2020-23) and Milwaukee Bucks (2023-26) earned him a place on the league’s top 15 coaches of all-time list a couple of years ago, and he’s had phenomenal success most coaches can only dream of having. Only five coaches in NBA history have more victories than Rivers’ 1,194 regular-season wins. Only Popovich (1,390), Don Nelson (1,335), Lenny Wilkens (1,332), Jerry Sloan (1,221) and Pat Riley (1,210) have more. He’s coached the fourth-most games in league history (2,060). Among coaches with at least 1,000 games on the sidelines, Rivers has the ninth-highest regular-season win percentage (58.0 percent). A former staffer under Rivers said that he doesn’t feel Rivers gets as much credit as he should for his offensive creativity with X’s and O’s. “I used to look at his play designs and think, ‘Oh, that puts the defense in a real tough spot,’” former Clippers video coordinator Mo Dakhil told The Athletic .
HoopsHype →
Houston Rockets · Aug 14, 11:05 UTC · via New York Times
The real enduring secret of Mike D'Antoni's success is how he leaned into smaller, faster lineups and 3-point shots and allowed talented guards to thrive. It’s not like he was the first to discover the value of floor spacing or the added value of a 3-pointer, but D’Antoni was the one who weaponized it into an entire system. He did so, in part, by having the humility to get out of his stars’ way. “He saw his job as maximizing the players and letting the players be the centerpiece,” said former Rockets and Sixers executive Daryl Morey, who paired with D’Antoni for four seasons in Houston .
HoopsHype →

item.title: 3 coaching rumors — Dallas Mavericks (Aug 13)
item.description:
Dallas Mavericks · Aug 13, 18:09 UTC · via New York Times
When Dallas Mavericks general manager Mike Schmitz called to pick Dusty May’s brain about Michigan’s three NBA Draft prospects on the morning of May 24, he asked one question that got the ball rolling toward May leaving the school he’d just won a championship with to coach the Mavericks. “Would you have any interest in this job?” Schmitz’s timing was perfect, May told him. May had just returned home from the Big Ten’s spring meetings, where the league’s coaches met to discuss, among other things, the state of the game. “I was so excited for Big Ten meetings, like ‘we’re going to find some solutions,’” May told The Athletic this week. “I go there and I was just like, ‘Oh my God, nothing’s getting fixed. Ever.’”
HoopsHype →
Dallas Mavericks · Aug 13, 18:09 UTC · via New York Times
The other factor that made it easier for May was how much of a college coach’s time is spent on fundraising and administrative duties that took him away from focusing on his team. “I just spent so much more of my time doing everything but coaching,” he said. May’s favorite parts of the job were the actual basketball and the people side, building relationships with his players. The NBA offered an opportunity to shift more focus there. Another of his favorite aspects of coaching in college was the ability to choose your team, serving as your own general manager.
HoopsHype →
Dallas Mavericks · Aug 13, 18:09 UTC · via New York Times
If May ever decided to return to college, he would be extremely coveted, just like Rick Pitino and John Calipari were after taking their shots in the NBA in the late 1990s. May was asked if he’d ever consider a return. “I hope not, because that would mean I did sh—y here,” May said, laughing. “I’d like to win and stay.”
HoopsHype →

training camps are considered among the toughest in the NBA, but Simone Fontecchio had already experienced something even more demanding under Dusko Ivanovic at Baskonia . “Last year, Spoelstra asked me whether Miami’s training camp was the hardest I had ever experienced,” Fontecchio told the YouTube channel La Giornata Tipo. “I said that, if it made him happy, I could say it was. In the NBA, yes. But not in my entire life.”
HoopsHype →
Miami Heat · Aug 02, 17:03 UTC · via EuroHoops.net
Fontecchio joined Baskonia immediately after representing Italy at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021. His Olympic campaign ended on August 8, while Ivanovic’s preseason began two days later. “I was still in Japan and had to stop in Italy, so I very timidly asked Dusko if I could arrive later,” he recalled. “He said: ‘Of course. We start on the 10th, but you can come on the 12th.’” After a 13-hour journey, Fontecchio reached Vitoria around lunchtime and assumed he would be given time to recover. “Dusko told me: ‘Go and complete your physical tests. Practice is scheduled for 4 p.m., but don’t worry—we’ll move it to 6 p.m. so you can join us.’”

"He said, 'Well, they don't -- they don't want to do the fourth year.' Now, this was when it was this was a different regime, and they were they were quabbling over the fourth year. "And I said, 'Steve, do you have any idea how much money that the Madison Square Garden operation has with Cable Vision and all that?' ... He goes, 'Well, there's -- I don't know -- some reasons.' I said, 'I've heard your name with Golden State a little bit. ... That is a conference finals team, like right now. If you want to go to a team ready to win, that's the place you should go if you can.'"

Los Angeles Lakers · Jul 17, 18:35 UTC · via New York Times
Nathan Bubes walked into the makeshift locker room at halftime of the Minnesota Timberwolves ’ Las Vegas Summer League opener against New Orleans with a message. “I told them we need to take a deep breath,” Bubes said. “And as I said that, I was like, ‘So do I.'” Summer league is a chance for players with a lower profile to get noticed and try to earn a spot on a roster, either as a full-time or two-way player. It also offers that opportunity to young coaches, who are typically entrusted with running games and practices as they try to work their way up the ladder. This is the chance Bubes has been dreaming about since he entered the NBA as a barely paid intern with the Los Angeles Lakers in 2018. Long encouraged by those around him to go into the front-office side of basketball operations, Bubes has been determined to make his way in coaching. Now, as the leader of the Wolves’ summer team, he is charged with furthering the development of Joan Beringer and Rocco Zikarsky, getting second-round draft pick Isaiah Evans up to speed and helping to evaluate other players, including promising point guard Zyon Pullin, two-way forward Enrique Freeman and sharpshooter Nate Santos.
HoopsHype →
Minnesota Timberwolves · Jul 17, 18:35 UTC · via New York Times
Bubes has long been the right-hand man for Wolves head coach Chris Finch, winning him over when both were in New Orleans and then serving as his chief of staff in Minnesota. He’s done everything asked of him, including serving as the man on the hot seat during games to determine if Finch should challenge a call, spending a season as an assistant with the G League team in Iowa and easing Finch’s day-to-day operations by helping with planning, organizing and communicating with the rest of the staff. “He deserves the opportunity just because of how important he’s been to me,” Finch said. “So, I figured this was the summer to do that.”

item.description:
Milwaukee Bucks · Jul 15, 20:56 UTC · via Milwaukee Journal-Sentinel
Mike Budenholzer was a coach who believed in routine and a process of team building that had proved successful. A big part of that were his “break breads,” which were team dinners or gatherings, win or lose, on the road . “Break bread after every game – after every game – every game that we played that we stayed over there was a place for all of the players and all of the families to eat,” Giannis Antetokounmpo said. “And it was always packed. Everybody went. Because we knew it was part of our culture. Everybody had to show face. [With] all these things, there's a lot of owners that are like, 'you're spending money,' the food budget and all that goes up. Like a million dollars to $2.5 so they might not like it. But in order for you to win, you gotta spend money.”

Look, ‘We need to do this. We’re going to try to do team dinners, we’re going to try to do all these different things so the team could feel we’re all in this together.’ I think that ended up working well. I think Bud did a great job, but I also think the players understood what it meant and the players bought into it.“

Mike Budenholzer: “That team was ready. They had what it took. So I think you just hopefully create an environment and space where they can be their best. All those decisions, all the things we did to create culture, just let them know we care about them and put them in a position to be great. And I'm very appreciative that those guys – I think they do. They all love to talk about it. I think there's a lot of fond memories and appreciation. That's the stuff I love.
